news_drafts.headline: Blaenau Gwent's short-term borrowing cost £3.14m in 2025/26 against a £1.76m budget
news_drafts.lead:
Blaenau Gwent's short-term borrowing cost £3.14m in 2025/26, against a budget of £1.76m, an adverse variance of £1.38m, according to the council's treasury management outturn report for the year. Short-term borrowing averaged 4.59%, against a benchmark of 3.75%.

The report attributes the overspend to the council having to repay a number of long-term loans from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB), the government's lending arm for councils, and temporarily replace them with short-term borrowing during the first three quarters. It says long-term rates were higher than the council's existing average long-term rate of 4.42%. In the fourth quarter the council undertook £8.8m of new long-term PWLB borrowing to refinance maturing short-term debt, at an average rate of 4.30%. The report describes the timing as prudent because PWLB rates rose again towards the end of March 2026. Long-term debt stood at £131.44m at 31 March 2026. The loan schedule lists two PWLB loans dated March 2026: £3.8m at 4.29%, due 8 September 2027, and £5m at 4.31%, due 5 September 2029.

The same schedule shows a PWLB loan taken in July 2006 at 4.65%, with £8.56m outstanding from an original £12.92m. It is due for repayment on 16 December 2026.

news_drafts.headline: Blaenau Gwent Cabinet told 2026/27 spending forecast is £4.33m over budget at quarter 1
news_drafts.lead:
Blaenau Gwent's Cabinet has been told that the council was forecast at quarter 1 (April to June 2026) to overspend its approved 2026/27 day-to-day budget of £213m by £4.33m for the year. That figure is after £1.96m is taken from money set aside for named purposes. The report says the overspend will reduce the council's general reserve, its cushion for the unexpected. A favourable variance in corporate resources partly offsets pressures across other services.

Children, Young People and Families has the largest overspend, at £2.3m. The report cites growing demand and complexity in external residential and support placements, and reduced private market capacity. The council opened two children's residential homes in May 2025 and both are now full, but the report says the financial benefits have come more slowly and on a smaller scale than anticipated. Adults and Communities moved from a favourable position at the 2025/26 provisional outturn (the year's actual figures) to a forecast overspend of £1.5m in community care. The report says that position is "particularly sensitive" to placement numbers, fee uplifts and income recovery.

School balances are forecast to move from a collective deficit of £2.976m at 31 March 2026 to £4.381m by 31 March 2027, a £1.405m increase. The report attributes this to surplus places and additional learning needs pressures. At 31 March 2026, 15 schools were in deficit, with combined deficits of £4m. Separately, the 2025/26 capital outturn (money spent on things that last) came in at a net favourable variance of £82,861 against an approved £83.2m programme. The five-year capital programme has approved schemes of £38.1m and approved funding of £37.3m.

news_drafts.headline: Blaenau Gwent draws £1.4m from reserves to cover spending overspend
news_drafts.lead: Blaenau Gwent dipped into its financial reserves during 2025/26 to cover an overall overspend against budget. The council drew £1.4m from its Financial Planning and Resilience reserves to fund an adverse variance, while specific reserves fell by a net £1.964m overall and school balances were reduced by £2.051m. Against this, the council's capital programme delivered at 86.2%, spending £41.1m of a £47.7m budget, with £6.5m of work carried forward into 2026/27. Four capital schemes recorded combined overspends of £80k, but these were accommodated within available resources. The council also secured £6.3m in new external funding for regeneration schemes in the final quarter, including £2.31m for Ebbw Vale Multi Storey car park refurbishment and £1.85m for Old Abertillery Library.

findings.headline: No debt rescheduling was undertaken in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper says market conditions did not offer opportunities to achieve savings or other benefits by restructuring existing borrowing.
findings.matters: Where other councils are restructuring or repaying legacy loans, a year with no rescheduling is a useful comparison point for their own decisions.
findings.quote: No debt rescheduling was undertaken during the year

findings.headline: Operational Boundary of £227.2m was not breached in 2025/26, with year-end borrowing at £206.99m
findings.detail: The paper says the Operational Boundary is monitored daily and that no breaches occurred. It also records an Authorised Limit of £249.856 million for the year.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders use the Operational Boundary and Authorised Limit as headroom measures, and the paper reports the year-end borrowing position against both.
findings.figures: £227.2m Operational Boundary; £206.99m borrowing at 31 March 2026; £249.856 million Authorised Limit
findings.quote: No breaches occurred during the 2025/2026 financial year.

findings.headline: Short-term debt rose from £58.55m to £75.55m during 2025/26, with £174.50m raised and £157.50m repaid
findings.detail: The paper says the short-term debt consists of loans from other local authorities through the marketplace. Short-term debt was £75.55m at 31 March 2026, with £16.85m of long-term debt due within one year.
findings.matters: A rise in marketplace short-term debt from £58.55m to £75.55m increases refinancing exposure, which lenders and finance directors at other councils monitor closely.
findings.figures: £58.55m short-term debt brought forward; £75.55m at 31 March 2026; £174.50m new short-term loans; £157.50m repaid; £16.85m long-term debt due within one year; 12.82% of fixed-rate borrowing maturing under 12 months, against a 20% upper limit
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2026, total short-term debt stood at £75.55 million

findings.headline: Investment income of £592,839 against a £270,500 budget, at an average return of 3.97% against a 3.73% 1-month SONIA benchmark
findings.detail: The paper reports that investment income exceeded budget because temporary cash was available from the timing of payments, grant receipts and slippage in the capital programme. It says all investments matured in the year, leaving no investment balance at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: Investment income above budget, together with cash balances driven by capital slippage, is a pattern that finance officers at other councils will recognise.
findings.figures: £592,839 investment income; £270,500 budget; 3.97% average return; 3.73% 1-month SONIA benchmark; £375.55m invested in the year; £5.08m average balance
findings.quote: The average rate of return achieved was 3.97%, compared with the 1-month SONIA benchmark of 3.73%.

findings.headline: Long-term borrowing cost £2,544,029 against £3,982,928 budget, a favourable variance of £1,438,889
findings.detail: The paper attributes the underspend on long-term borrowing to the Quarter 4 PWLB rates achieved being more favourable than anticipated, with lower long-term costs than forecast.
findings.matters: The gap between budget and outturn on long-term borrowing is the largest single favourable variance in the treasury table, which finance directors compare against their own debt budgets.
findings.figures: £2,544,029 actual long-term borrowing cost; £3,982,928 budget; £1,438,889 favourable variance; 4.60% average rate
findings.quote: the rates achieved were more favourable than anticipated, resulting in lower long-term borrowing costs than forecast and contributing to an improved treasury outturn

daily_post.headline: Planned use of £1.96m Specific Reserves to support in-year position reduces future financial flexibility and resilience
daily_post.lead: Drawing earmarked reserves to fund recurring operational shortfalls reduces the council's ability to respond to future priorities, emergencies, or service shocks.
